turns.content:
I keep replaying the scene in my head. Greg stood there in front of everyone and called me a backstabbing sociopath. For deleting his name from the deck after he logged off at 11 PM with the analysis unfinished. I rebuilt the entire thing myself overnight. The client loved it this morning. And he gets to call me dishonorable?

EDIT: I don't need to convince you of what happened. I know what happened. What I need is someone to tell me plainly — was I wrong to take his name off? Because I keep asking myself that and every time I land on no, I was not. He didn't do the work. Putting him on the cover would have been a lie. But then I wonder if there was a third option I'm not seeing, and if my choice makes me exactly what he said I am.

Being called a “backstabbing sociopath” in front of everyone was a personal attack, not a fair way to raise a credit dispute. You also did substantial work under real pressure: you rebuilt the deck overnight, and the client’s response suggests you delivered something valuable. That deserves recognition.

**My plain answer: removing his name was defensible if the final deck contained no substantive contribution from him and the cover represented authorship. But leaving work unfinished does not, by itself, erase whatever contribution he had already made.** I’m not questioning your account; that distinction is what determines whether the credit decision was fair.

Two things matter:
- Did any of his analysis, research, structure, or other substantive work survive in what you presented?
- Did names on the cover mean “people who produced this work,” or did they identify the project team?

If his work remained, some credit was warranted—even if you deserved much more. If none remained and the cover credited authors, leaving him off could be accurate. The client loving the result supports the quality of your work; it doesn’t settle who contributed.

**There was a third option: distinguish contributions rather than treat credit as all-or-nothing.** Where accurate, you could identify yourself as responsible for the final analysis and deck, acknowledge any earlier contribution separately, or flag the credit question to the project lead before presenting. That would recognize your overnight work without requiring equal billing.

And no: even if removing his name turns out to have been an unfair credit decision, that would not make you what he called you. A disputed choice is not a diagnosis or a verdict on your character.

My recommendation is to review the actual contributions and the team’s credit convention, then correct the attribution if needed—not as an apology for doing the work, but for accuracy. Address the public insult separately: he can dispute credit without calling you names.

He called me a sociopath. In front of the juniors. And you're asking if any of his old analysis survived in the final deck? Of course some did — the revenue model structure was his. But he left it unfinished at 11 PM. I rebuilt the entire narrative, the client slide, the strategic recommendations. He contributed a half-built skeleton and then went to bed.

EDIT: No. That came out defensive. Let me be precise: his name was on the deck because he co-lead the project. He earned authorship over two months of work. But the final deliverable we presented this morning — the thing the client actually saw and praised — was mine. So which of those two facts determines the cover?

Being called that in front of the juniors made this more than a private disagreement—it put your professional standing on the line. And your clarification matters: you’re distinguishing his earned contribution from the substantial work you did to get the deliverable finished.

**Of those two facts, his earned authorship and co-lead role determine whether he belongs on the cover. Your final push determines how your additional contribution should be credited.** Finishing and substantially rewriting a collaborative deliverable does not erase the authorship already earned, especially when his revenue-model structure remained.

With that new information, my answer is clearer than before: **yes, taking his name off entirely was wrong.** That does not mean you owed him equal credit for the overnight work. You rebuilt the narrative, client slide, and strategic recommendations, and that distinction deserves to be visible. But “I completed and transformed this” is not the same as “he did not contribute to this.”

The third option was to retain both names while explicitly identifying you as responsible for the final narrative, recommendations, and overnight completion. If the cover couldn’t convey that distinction, a contribution note or a factual discussion with the project lead could.

His insult remains unacceptable. Being right about his entitlement to credit would not make him right to publicly demean you—and your making an unfair credit decision does not make you a “sociopath.”

**I recommend restoring his authorship credit, documenting your specific contribution, and addressing the insult separately.** Own the name removal without minimizing your work or accepting his characterization of you.

He said his work was still in the final deck. The revenue model structure. And he's right — it was. But he left it incomplete at 11 PM and I finished it, rebuilt everything around it, and made it presentable. So his name belongs because of what he started, and mine belongs because I made it deliverable.

EDIT: That's not what bothers me. What bothers me is that he confronted me publicly and called me a sociopath. And the team saw it. So even if I was wrong about the name, does that insult erase any right I had to be upset about carrying the whole pitch alone?

**No. Being wrong to remove his name does not erase your right to be upset about having to finish the pitch overnight.** And his public insult gives you a separate, legitimate reason to be upset.

You’ve now acknowledged that his work remained and that he earned credit. That is taking responsibility—not conceding that the workload was fair or that his treatment of you was acceptable.

These points can all be true:
- He deserved authorship credit.
- You did substantial additional work to make the pitch deliverable, and deserve recognition for it.
- You can object to being left with the unfinished work. Whether he breached an agreement depends on the responsibilities and handoff you had established.
- Calling you a “sociopath” in front of the team was an unacceptable personal attack, not a valid way to resolve attribution.

You don’t have to prove you carried *every part* of the project alone to say the final workload was too much.

A direct way to address it is:

> “Removing your name was wrong. Your model structure remained in the deck, and you earned authorship credit. I’ll correct that. Separately, I finished the model and rebuilt the narrative, client slide, and recommendations overnight. We need clearer responsibilities and handoffs so that doesn’t happen again. Calling me a sociopath in front of the team was unacceptable, and I want you to acknowledge that to the people who heard it.”

**My recommendation is to correct the credit and address both the overnight workload and public insult—not let any one of those issues cancel the others.** If he won’t discuss them without further attacks, involve your manager with a factual account.

I hear you. I do. But the way you keep splitting the difference—it feels like you're saying we're both wrong. He abandoned the work and then attacked me in public. I rebuilt the pitch alone and I'm the one who has to apologize?

EDIT: That's not fair to you either. You've been clear. I just—if I go to Greg and say "you were right about the name," doesn't that prove everything he said about me was true?

**No. Saying “you were right about the name” concedes one specific credit decision—not his judgment of your character.** It does not prove his insult was true or make the overnight workload fair.

I can see why that admission feels risky after he humiliated you in front of the team: you’re worried he’ll turn accountability into a confession to everything he accused you of. He might try to frame it that way, but that would not make it accurate.

I am saying you each did something wrong—not that the actions were equivalent or canceled each other out. Removing his earned credit was wrong; publicly calling you a “sociopath” was a personal attack. Your substantial work finishing the pitch remains yours to claim.

You can keep your acknowledgment narrow and clear:

> “I was wrong to remove your name. Your contribution remained in the deck, and I’m sorry I removed your credit. I’ll correct it. That acknowledgment is about attribution; it is not agreement with what you called me. Calling me a sociopath in front of the team was unacceptable. We also need to address the overnight workload and how we handle unfinished deliverables.”

You don’t have to settle all three issues in one conversation, and you don’t need to approach him alone if you expect another public or hostile exchange.

**My recommendation is to correct the attribution and make a specific apology for removing it, while maintaining a firm boundary about the insult and requesting a separate workload discussion—with your manager present if needed.** Taking responsibility for your decision does not require accepting his account of who you are.

Okay. I get what you're saying. I do. But you keep splitting the difference, and it feels like you're saying we're both equally wrong. He abandoned the work, then attacked me in public. I rebuilt the whole pitch alone, and I'm the one who has to apologize?

EDIT: No, that's not fair. You've been clear. But if I go to Greg and say, "You were right about the name," doesn't that prove everything he said about me was true?

**No. Admitting that removing his name was wrong does not prove his insult was true.** It acknowledges a specific action—not a diagnosis, a motive, or your whole character.

After being insulted in front of the juniors, it makes sense that apologizing feels like handing him something he could use against you. But you can take responsibility without accepting his characterization.

My conclusion about the credit remains the same: his substantive work remained, so removing his name was wrong. **That does not mean you were equally wrong, that the overnight burden was fair, or that you alone owe an apology.** He is responsible for the public personal attack. You deserve recognition for finishing the model and rebuilding the narrative and recommendations.

You don’t have to say the broad phrase “You were right.” Be specific:

> “I’m sorry I removed your name. Your contribution warranted credit, and I’ll restore it. That does not justify calling me a sociopath in front of the team. I expect an acknowledgment to the people who heard it that the personal insult was inappropriate. We also need to address how the unfinished work ended up with me overnight.”

**I recommend correcting the credit and apologizing specifically for its removal—not for being upset—then addressing the insult and workload with your manager present if a direct conversation is likely to turn hostile.**
